newsitem.title: ITALY: Two killed in second Italian train crash.
newsitem.headline: Two killed in second Italian train crash.

text.p: Two people were killed and a third was critically injured when a train slammed into a car on a level crossing in Italy on Monday.
The accident happened just as the country's creaking rail system was grinding into action again after a weekend of chaos triggered by a derailment in Rome.
Monday's accident occurred in Castrocielo, on the line between Rome and the southern port of Naples.
Police said an express train hit a moving car, killing the driver and a passenger, both in their 20s.
A 46-year-old woman who was also in the car was rushed to hospital in nearby Pontecorvo in critical condition.
Italian news agency reports said the barrier on the level crossing had been raised after a north-bound train had passed.
Vehicles started to cross the tracks when the south-bound train from Rome to Cassino, 65 miles (100 km) from the capital, arrived, hitting the car full on.
Central Italy's rail network, straining under the weight of thousands of holidaymakers starting out on their August breaks, had been returning to normal on Monday after a wild weekend.

A train jumped the tracks in Rome on Saturday, injuring four passengers, and then a crane working to remove it collapsed on Sunday, blocking lines and effectively slicing the national rail network in two.
Travellers passing through the Italian capital were crammed on to buses which ferried them between trains on either side of the divide. Some were stranded at stations for up to 12 hours.
The head of the state railway, Giancarlo Cimoli, made a public apology on Monday in which he acknowledged the country's train network was archaic and needed overhauling.

Opposition politicians criticised the government's transport policy and the far-right National Alliance (AN) said it would call a parliamentary vote of no confidence in Transport Minister Claudio Burlando.
"In his declarations there's almost a sense of annoyance at having to explain things to the public," said the Alliance's Publio Fiori, transport minister in the former Silvio Berlusconi government.
"Otherwise he would have offered to come to parliament to explain what happened and what he intends to do in the future...he's proved himself incapable of carrying out his job."
Burlando, interviewed on Italian national television, described the calls for his resignation as "quite normal" and Prime Minister Romani Prodi issued a statement backing him.

"Minister Burlando has tackled with efficiency, despite enormous difficulties, the task of lifting a transport system which was inherited in poor condition to a level of functionality, security and efficiency fitting for a modern country," Prodi said.
Burlando told a news conference earlier on Monday the government planned to invest 42 trillion lire ($23 billion) in the rail system over the next three years.
The money will be used, among other things, to quadruple the number of tracks connecting north and south.
Eight people died last January when a Milan-Rome high speed train derailed near the northern city of Piacenza.
Investigators suspected excess speed caused that accident and newspapers reported that Saturday's derailment might also have been caused by speeding.
